brief: Quality gates, and why approval is not the same as quality

slots.subtitle: Six things a sign-off actually tells you, and the one it never does.
slots.item1: Why a green checklist is a coverage claim, not a quality one
slots.item2: The control nobody can justify and nobody will remove
slots.coverNote: The last page is what no process can supply

slots.body: A sign-off records that somebody with authority looked at it, which is a fact about a process rather than about the work. Most approval gates measure whether the right person saw it in time, and almost none measure whether it was any good.
slots.p1Body: That the process was followed, on the date it was followed.
slots.p2Body: Anything the approver was not equipped to notice.
slots.p3Body: One person whose job is to disagree, named in advance.

slots.body: It is excellent at the failures somebody already met and blind to everything else. That is not a criticism — it is the point — but a team that treats a green checklist as a quality signal has confused coverage with confidence.
slots.p1Body: One line per incident. That is how the list earns its length.
slots.p2Body: An item nothing has tripped in a year is ceremony.
slots.p3Body: The list handles the known. A person handles the rest.

slots.body: Adding a second pair of eyes to the same review produces agreement, not coverage. What finds different problems is a different question — one person reading for correctness and another for whether it should exist at all.
slots.p1Body: Correctness, clarity, scope. Not 'have a look'.
slots.p2Body: A fresh reviewer sees more than a second simultaneous one.
slots.p3Body: Three reviewers is a committee and decides nothing.

slots.body: A control added after one incident taxes every unrelated piece of work for years, and nobody ever proposes removing it because removing a safeguard is an unpopular thing to be wrong about. The cost is invisible and permanent.
slots.p1Body: Specifically. If nobody can, it is habit.
slots.p2Body: The queue is the cost, not the review itself.
slots.p3Body: Set a date to reconsider, or it is forever.

slots.body: Every gate before release tests the thing under conditions you chose. The first real information arrives when somebody who was not involved tries to do something you did not anticipate, which is the only test that was never designed to pass.
slots.p1Body: Real conditions, small blast radius, immediate signal.
slots.p2Body: What they do beats what they say by a wide margin.
slots.p3Body: Confidence comes from being able to undo it in a minute.

slots.body: Every control here filters. None of them creates, and a process built entirely from filters produces work that is defensible, inoffensive and slightly worse each round, because nothing in it rewards the thing that would have made it interesting.
slots.p1Body: And, reliably, some of the best along with it.
slots.p2Body: Process cannot supply that. It can only protect it.
slots.p3Body: The gates should serve them, not replace them.

slots.stampSub: set a date, or it is forever
slots.body: Pick the oldest control in your process and ask what specific failure it stops. If nobody can answer, you have found this quarter's easiest saving.
slots.closingLine: A process made only of filters produces work that is defensible and slightly worse each round.
slots.signoff: The queue is the cost, not the review
